newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Experts see long-term merit in EMU rules.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Experts see long-term merit in EMU rules.

text.p: The entry targets for Europe's single currency club won a positive endorsement on Thursday in a Reuters poll of how countries are shaping up for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Twenty-four out of 45 European economists surveyed on the likelihood of EMU being launched on time said the rules laid down in the Maastricht treaty were either likely, or very likely, to promote sustainable economic convergence in the long term.
Another 13 said the criteria would be "quite likely" to help promote long-term convergence among member states and only the remaining eight thought the criteria would not have the desired effect.
"Economies will converge because actual monetary union will promote economic convergence," said Peter van den Houte, senior economist at Bank Brussels Lambert.

"Almost irrespective of Maastricht, there is convergence across Europe because of the internationalisation of the world economy and we do, to all intents and purposes, operate in a free trade area. These are promoting convergence already," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America in London.

In order to gain entry to EMU, potential members must achieve ambitious economic targets during 1997 relating to inflation, interest rates, debt and deficit levels, designed to achieve stability for the nascent euro currency.

But the rules are stringent and economists fear that the criteria will be fudged beyond the terms of the treaty by borderline states to attain membership. Even Germany is expected by many experts to miss at least two of the criteria, raising the prospect of a delay to the EMU launch.
The economists polled in the Reuters survey also thought the chances were low that a major crisis would strike EMU in its early years.
Among 41 contributors who gave an opinion, the average likelihood they gave for a major crisis erupting in the first two years was just less than one in four.
"So much has been invested in it, no one will even admit to a crisis," said Han de Jong, head of international bond research at ABN-Amro in Amsterdam.

"A crisis would depend on who is in EMU. With a broader membership the chances are much higher than if only the hard core were to join at the beginning," said Carlo Favero, professor of econometrics at Bocconi University in Milan.
